**Setup.** Let $x_i^T$ denote the $i$th row of $X$ (so $x_i \in \mathbb{R}^n$), and $S_i = \{j : X_{ij} \neq 0\}$ with $|S_i| = q_i$. Note $D = \operatorname{diag}(X^TX) = \sum_i \operatorname{diag}(x_i x_i^T)$ and $X^T Q^{-1} X = \sum_i \frac{1}{q_i} x_i x_i^T$. Thus

$$M = D - X^T Q^{-1} X = \sum_{i=1}^m \underbrace{\left[\operatorname{diag}(x_i x_i^T) - \frac{1}{q_i}\, x_i x_i^T\right]}_{M_i}.$$

---

**Key Lemma.** *Each $M_i$ is positive semidefinite.*

*Proof.* For any $z \in \mathbb{R}^n$,

$$z^T M_i\, z = \sum_{j \in S_i} X_{ij}^2\, z_j^2 \;-\; \frac{1}{q_i}\!\left(\sum_{j \in S_i} X_{ij}\, z_j\right)^{\!2}.$$

By Cauchy–Schwarz applied to the vectors $(X_{ij}\, z_j)_{j \in S_i}$ and $(1,\ldots,1) \in \mathbb{R}^{q_i}$:

$$\left(\sum_{j \in S_i} X_{ij}\, z_j\right)^{\!2} \leq \left(\sum_{j \in S_i} X_{ij}^2\, z_j^2\right)\cdot q_i.$$

Hence $z^T M_i\, z \geq 0$. Moreover, equality holds if and only if $X_{ij}\, z_j = \lambda_i$ (a constant) for all $j \in S_i$. $\square$

---

**(b) Positive semidefinite.** Since $M = \sum_i M_i$ and each $M_i \succeq 0$, we conclude:

> **$D - X^T Q^{-1} X$ is always positive semidefinite** under the stated hypotheses (no null columns, $q_i \geq 1$). No additional conditions are required.

---

**(a) Positive definite.** Since each $M_i \succeq 0$, we have $z^T M\, z = 0$ if and only if $z^T M_i\, z = 0$ for every $i$. By the equality condition in the lemma, this means:

$$z^T M\, z = 0 \iff \forall\, i,\; \exists\, \lambda_i \text{ such that } X_{ij}\, z_j = \lambda_i \;\text{ for all } j \in S_i.$$

That is, $z$ lies in the null space of $M$ if and only if, within each row $i$, the products $X_{ij}\,z_j$ are all equal (to some row-constant $\lambda_i$). Equivalently, $z$ satisfies the homogeneous linear system

$$X_{ij}\, z_j = X_{ik}\, z_k \quad \text{for all } i \text{ and all } j, k \in S_i.$$

Therefore:

> **$D - X^T Q^{-1} X$ is positive definite if and only if the only vector $z \in \mathbb{R}^n$ satisfying "$X_{ij}\,z_j$ is constant over $j \in S_i$ for each row $i$" is $z = 0$.**

**Graph-theoretic characterization.** Form the bipartite graph $B$ with row-vertices $\{r_1,\ldots,r_m\}$ and column-vertices $\{c_1,\ldots,c_n\}$, where $(r_i, c_j)$ is an edge iff $X_{ij} \neq 0$. The system $X_{ij}\,z_j = \lambda_i$ admits a nontrivial solution if and only if, in every connected component of $B$, value-propagation around all cycles is consistent. Specifically, for a cycle $r_{i_0}\!-\!c_{j_0}\!-\!r_{i_1}\!-\!c_{j_1}\!-\!\cdots\!-\!r_{i_{p-1}}\!-\!c_{j_{p-1}}\!-\!r_{i_0}$ in $B$, the consistency condition is:

$$\prod_{l=0}^{p-1} \frac{X_{i_{l+1 \bmod p},\; j_l}}{X_{i_l,\; j_l}} \;=\; 1.$$

(These conditions need only be checked on a set of fundamental cycles, since the log-product is additive over cycle composition.)

> **$M$ is positive definite if and only if every connected component of the bipartite graph of $X$ contains at least one cycle for which the above product is not equal to $1$.**

In particular, if any connected component of $B$ is a tree (acyclic), then $M$ is singular. If $X$ is a $\{0,1\}$-matrix, all ratios are $1$, every cycle product equals $1$, and $M$ is **never** positive definite — the vector that is constant on each connected component of the column graph always lies in the null space (generalizing the fact that the graph Laplacian has $\mathbf{1}$ in its kernel).

---

**Summary.**

- **(b)** $D - X^T Q^{-1} X \succeq 0$ **unconditionally** (given the hypotheses: no null columns, $q_i \geq 1$). This follows from the Cauchy–Schwarz decomposition $M = \sum_i M_i$ with each $M_i \succeq 0$.

- **(a)** $D - X^T Q^{-1} X \succ 0$ **if and only if** there is no nonzero $z \in \mathbb{R}^n$ such that $X_{ij}\,z_j$ is constant within each row. Equivalently, every connected component of the bipartite graph of $X$ (rows vs.\ columns, edges at nonzero entries) contains a cycle along which the product of the weight ratios $\prod X_{i_{l+1}j_l}/X_{i_l j_l}$ differs from $1$.
